[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance describes how Platform Engineering authors the security template component for a Golden Path bundle in conformance with [PTN-SEC-GOV-001](../../../../patterns/security/governance/PTN-SEC-GOV-001-golden-path-security-template-pattern.md). It covers the authoring sequence for each mandatory security manifest, the OPA policy validation procedure, and the pre-submission verification required before ARB approval.

A security template is the security configuration component of a Golden Path bundle. It is one of five components required for ARB submission. It delivers the Kubernetes manifests — NetworkPolicy, cert-manager Certificate, dedicated ServiceAccount with workload identity, and pod security context — that satisfy NIST SP 800-53 r5 controls (SC-7, SC-8, AC-6, IA-9, CM-6/CM-7) at the workload level for every service instantiated from the path. For HIPAA-scoped paths, satisfying these NIST controls satisfies the corresponding HIPAA §164.312 technical safeguard requirements via the regulatory overlay mapping in PTN-SEC-GOV-001.
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#business-value]

### Business Value

- Security Architecture reviews the security template once at the catalog level; every service on the path inherits the reviewed configuration without individual service security review
- OPA Layer 3 checks pass on the first pipeline run because the manifests are pre-validated before publication — teams do not discover security policy violations during their first deployment
- NIST 800-53 r5 control evidence (SC-7 network isolation, SC-8/SC-17 TLS via cert-manager, AC-6/CM-7 non-root containers and minimal capabilities, AC-6/IA-9 workload identity) is produced structurally — it is not asserted; it is verified by OPA policy on every build. For HIPAA-scoped paths this simultaneously produces §164.312 technical safeguard evidence

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#target-audience]

### Target Audience

- **Primary**: Platform Engineering engineers authoring or updating a Golden Path security template
- **Secondary**: Security Architecture members reviewing security templates as part of ARB package review
- **Stakeholders**: Compliance teams who rely on OPA check results as security control evidence; product engineering teams who inherit the security template via the path scaffold

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#applicable-scenarios]

#### Applicable Scenarios

- Authoring the security template for a new Golden Path concurrent with the application scaffold and CI/CD pipeline template
- Updating an existing security template when a path version introduces new security requirements (e.g., a regulatory change, a new OPA policy check, a CVE patch)
- Promoting a path from HIPAA scope to FedRAMP Moderate scope — additional security template manifests required (SC-8(1) FIPS-validated cryptography, stricter SC-7 egress scope)
- Onboarding a CMS Medicaid/Medicare path requiring ARC-AMPE compliance — declare `compliance_scope: arc-ampe,hipaa` in `security-template-manifest.yaml`; all four ZTA control categories required; PSA `restricted` mode is the standard for ARC-AMPE namespaces
page_texts.9:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#scope-boundaries]

#### Scope Boundaries

- **In Scope**: The four mandatory security manifest files, the security template manifest, and OPA Layer 3 validation
- **Out of Scope**: Cluster-level security controls (covered by PTN-SEC-K8S-001, PTN-SEC-K8S-004 — these are prerequisites the security template builds on, not content it defines); the other four Golden Path bundle components (scaffold, CI/CD, Terraform, Verification Contract); the exception process for teams needing to deviate from the security template (GUID-GOV-PROC-002)

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#business-context]

### Business Context

The security template is the mechanism by which Zero Trust Architecture principles and regulatory compliance requirements (HIPAA, ARC-AMPE, FedRAMP Moderate) become structurally unavoidable for services built from the path. Without it, network policies, TLS certificate management, workload identity, and pod security configuration are team responsibilities — authored once per service, by engineers with varying security expertise, reviewed individually by Security Architecture. This model produces inconsistent security posture across equivalent services and violates ZTA principles (implicit network trust, shared identity, unverified communication) by default. It cannot scale to catalog-based or autonomous development speeds.

A security template authored once and reviewed by Security Architecture at the catalog level provides security assurance for the entire fleet of services on the path. The review investment scales inversely with adoption: one review covers twenty services, or two hundred.

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

The security template manifests are Nunjucks-parameterized YAML files stored at `catalog/security-templates/{path-id}/manifests/`. They use the same `${{ values.variable }}` expression syntax as the application scaffold. The scaffold runner merges these manifests into the `skeleton/{service_name}/k8s/` directory at instantiation time. Teams receive all security manifests pre-wired from the first commit.

The manifests are validated through the Enterprise Architecture Verification Strategy's four-layer architecture — each layer is an obligation on the security template author, not an external check applied afterward:

- **Layer 1 (Structural Conformance Gate)**: File presence checks confirm that `networkpolicy.yaml`, `certificate.yaml`, and `serviceaccount.yaml` exist in `k8s/` at CI/CD build time. The build is blocked if any required artifact is absent. The author verifies the file set locally before pushing.
- **Layer 2 (Fitness Functions)**: Behavioral validation is run after the merged artifact set is applied to a staging environment. **Layer 2a (Network Isolation fitness function)**: a test request from an unauthorized namespace is sent and the response confirms the NetworkPolicy blocks it; result saved as `network-isolation-{path-id}-{version}.txt`. **Layer 2b (Certificate Issuance fitness function)**: the cert-manager `Certificate` resource status is inspected to confirm `Ready=True` with the path-approved issuer reference (not self-signed); result saved as `cert-issuance-{path-id}-{version}.txt`. Both results are submitted to the compliance evidence store before ARB submission.
- **Layer 3 (Policy-as-Code)**: OPA/Rego policies (PTN-INFRA-GOV-002) evaluate the merged artifact set before deployment. The GP-001 policy bundle defines checks OPA-001 through OPA-007. The security template author **co-defines the OPA assertion field paths and expected values** with the Verification Contract author (GUID-GOV-IMPL-001 Phase 4) — the manifest author holds the knowledge of which YAML fields the assertions must evaluate.
- **Layer 4 (Runtime Monitors)**: Runtime drift detection requires design-time obligations. The security template author must declare `compliance_scope`, `path_id`, `environment`, and `team` labels on the NetworkPolicy and ServiceAccount, and ensure the ServiceAccount name follows the `{path_id}-{service_name}-sa` naming convention. These labels enable AWS Config / Azure Policy continuous drift monitors to attribute an alert to the correct path and team.

The `deployment.yaml` securityContext is a joint responsibility between the scaffold author (GUID-APP-IMPL-003) and the security template author. The scaffold author is responsible for creating `deployment.yaml`; the security template author is responsible for confirming that all six required `securityContext` fields are present. This coordination point must happen in Phase 5 of this guidance workflow before the final OPA validation run.

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

Without authoring guidance, security templates are produced with the most visible components (ESO, network policy) but miss the less obvious ones (workload identity ServiceAccount annotation, PSA namespace label, readOnlyRootFilesystem in securityContext). The ARB then reviews a template that appears complete based on file presence but fails several OPA checks because the content does not satisfy all policy assertions.

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#principle-1-author-concurrent-with-the-verification-contract-layer-3-checks]

#### Principle 1: Author Concurrent With the Verification Contract Layer 3 Checks

**Description:** Begin security template authoring only after the Verification Contract's Layer 3 OPA check IDs are finalized (GUID-GOV-IMPL-001 Phase 4). Each manifest is authored to satisfy specific OPA assertions — authoring before the assertions are defined produces manifests that may not satisfy what the contract ultimately requires.

**Rationale:** The OPA check defines the outcome; the manifest must satisfy it. If the manifest is authored first and the OPA check is defined later, the check may look for a different field value, annotation key, or resource name than the manifest provides. Pre-defining the check eliminates this rework pattern.

**Application:** Obtain the finalized OPA check YAML from the Verification Contract author before writing any manifest content. For each manifest section, reference the specific OPA check it must satisfy.
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#principle-2-every-security-control-must-be-machine-verifiable]

#### Principle 2: Every Security Control Must Be Machine-Verifiable

**Description:** Every NIST 800-53 r5 control addressed by the security template must be expressed as a manifest field that OPA can evaluate. Documentation-only controls (comments stating "TLS 1.3 is required") are not security controls — they are documentation.

**Rationale:** A comment in a YAML file does not enforce anything. The OPA check that verifies the same assertion does. Platform Engineering's responsibility is to translate every NIST control in scope into a manifest field and a corresponding OPA assertion, not to describe the requirement textually.

**Application:** For each NIST 800-53 r5 control in scope for the path (see PTN-SEC-GOV-001 Standards Alignment and Regulatory Compliance Overlays tables), identify the specific YAML field (or field absence) that enforces it via the ZTA tenet it implements. If no YAML field can enforce the control, escalate to the Verification Contract author to define a Layer 4 runtime monitor check instead. For paths with regulatory overlays (HIPAA, ARC-AMPE, FedRAMP Moderate, MARS-E), confirming the NIST control is satisfied is sufficient — the overlay mapping in the compliance metadata file (GUID-GOV-IMPL-002) records the regulatory → NIST control and ZTA tenet traceability.
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#principle-3-path-constants-are-not-team-inputs]

#### Principle 3: Path Constants Are Not Team Inputs

**Description:** Security-sensitive values — the `ClusterIssuer` name, the managed identity client ID, the Kafka CIDR range, the PSA enforcement level — are path constants declared in `security-template-manifest.yaml`. They are not exposed as scaffold parameters.

**Rationale:** A team that can override the `ClusterIssuer` to a self-signed issuer or change the PSA level to `privileged` can trivially disable the security controls the template is supposed to enforce. Security configuration must be structurally enforced by the template, not offered as a configuration choice.

**Application:** Before authoring each manifest, identify every value that has security implications. Move those values to path constants in `security-template-manifest.yaml`. The only parameterized values in security manifests are non-security-sensitive service identifiers: `service_name`, `namespace`, `team`.
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#principle-4-security-architecture-reviews-before-arb]

#### Principle 4: Security Architecture Reviews Before ARB

**Description:** The security template is the artifact that the Security Architecture team is most qualified to review. Obtain a Security Architecture sign-off before submitting to the ARB — not as part of the ARB session.

**Rationale:** The ARB is a governance gate, not a technical security review body. An ARB reviewer confirming that `networkpolicy.yaml` exists is not a security review. A Security Architecture engineer confirming that the CIDR ranges, cipher configuration, and PSA enforcement level are correct for the path's compliance scope is a security review. These are different activities.

**Application:** Schedule a Security Architecture review session at Phase 5 (before final OPA validation). Provide the OPA check YAML, the manifest set, and the compliance scope declaration. Obtain written sign-off before submitting the ARB package.

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#approach-1-opa-driven-manifest-authoring]

#### Approach 1: OPA-Driven Manifest Authoring

**Overview:** Start with the OPA check assertions rather than general Kubernetes YAML knowledge. Write each check assertion in plain English, then author the manifest field that satisfies it.

**When to Use:** For all new Golden Path security templates. Ensures all seven OPA checks are satisfied by construction rather than discovered as failures during validation.

**Steps:**
1. List all OPA check IDs from the Verification Contract Layer 3 section
2. For each check, write the plain-English assertion (e.g., "NetworkPolicy with podSelector matching the service label exists in the namespace")
3. Author the minimum YAML that satisfies the assertion
4. Run `opa eval` immediately after authoring each manifest — do not batch-validate at the end

**Benefits:** Catches field name errors, annotation key typos, and missing mandatory fields during authoring rather than at pre-submission validation.
page_texts.22:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#approach-2-adapt-from-an-existing-validated-template]

#### Approach 2: Adapt From an Existing Validated Template

**Overview:** When adding a new language variant to an existing path, or creating a closely related new path, take a validated security template as the starting point and adapt only the values that differ.

**When to Use:** When the new path or language variant shares the same compliance scope, cluster topology, and security requirements as an existing path with a validated security template.

**Steps:**
1. Copy the validated template from `catalog/security-templates/{existing-path-id}/`
2. Update `security-template-manifest.yaml` with the new path ID and any changed OPA check references
3. Review every manifest for path-constant values: update the managed identity client ID and any path-specific CIDR ranges
4. Run `opa eval` validation against the updated manifests to confirm all checks still pass

**Benefits:** Produces a correct security template quickly for path variants. Reduces the probability of missing a required manifest compared to authoring from scratch.

---
page_texts.23:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#best-practices]

### Best Practices

- **Validate after each manifest, not at the end.** `opa eval` against a single manifest file runs in seconds. Running it per-manifest surfaces errors immediately. Batch validation at the end of a 6-manifest authoring session produces a list of unrelated failures that are harder to diagnose.
- **Do not suppress OPA failures with `not_applicable` unless the path genuinely does not require the control.** Batch jobs legitimately do not require an ingress NetworkPolicy. REST microservices do. `not_applicable` is a documentation statement, not an OPA bypass. If the OPA check runs and the manifest fails, the check must be satisfied.
- **Test the NetworkPolicy egress rules against the actual cluster topology, not a diagram.** CIDR ranges that look correct on an architecture diagram may be wrong in the cluster. Verify Kafka broker and Key Vault endpoint CIDRs with the Platform Engineering networking team before hardcoding them as path constants.
- **Coordinate with the scaffold author early on `deployment.yaml` securityContext.** The securityContext fields are in the scaffold's `deployment.yaml`, not in the security template manifests. Discovering that `runAsUser: 1000` is missing from the scaffold after the security template OPA validation has already passed means re-running the scaffold validation as well.
- **Include a `SECURITY_CONTROLS.md` in the security template root** summarizing what each manifest enforces, the NIST 800-53 r5 control ID it satisfies, and (for HIPAA paths) the §164.312 specification it maps to. Teams instantiating the path will read this file; clear documentation prevents accidental removal of mandatory controls.
page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#common-pitfalls]

### Common Pitfalls

- **Authoring generic network policies that allow too much.** A `NetworkPolicy` with `{}` as the `podSelector` applies to all pods in the namespace — not just the service being scaffolded. Use explicit `matchLabels` scoped to `app: ${{ values.service_name }}`.
- **Certificate subject mismatch.** If `dnsNames` in `certificate.yaml` does not include the exact hostname the ingress controller serves, certificate validation fails at the client and TLS is effectively broken despite a valid cert-manager Certificate resource. Test with `kubectl get certificate` and `openssl s_client` against the staging ingress before ARB submission.
- **Forgetting the PSA namespace label.** PSA enforcement is a namespace-level configuration, not a pod-level configuration. A pod with a correct `securityContext` deployed into a namespace without the `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` label is not enforced by PSA. The `podsecurity-patch.yaml` applies this label; confirm it is applied to the target namespace in the staging validation environment.
- **Workload identity annotation uses the wrong client ID.** The `azure.workload.identity/client-id` annotation must match the federated identity credential configured in the AKS cluster for the service account. Using a placeholder or copy-paste error produces a silent failure — the pod starts, ESO fails to authenticate, and secrets are not synced. Validate ESO secret sync during Phase 5 staging validation.
- **Path constants embedded in comments, not in fields.** A comment that says `# TLS 1.3 required` does not enforce TLS 1.3. If an OPA check for TLS protocol configuration is in the Verification Contract, the enforcing manifest field must be present. Comments are documentation; OPA checks are enforcement.

---

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#authoring-workflow-overview]

### Authoring Workflow Overview

```
Phase 1: Prerequisites and Co-authoring Obligation
    → Co-define the Verification Contract Layer 3 OPA assertion field paths and expected values with the
      Verification Contract author (GUID-GOV-IMPL-001 Phase 4) — the security template author holds the
      knowledge of which manifest YAML fields the assertions must evaluate; this is co-authoring, not
      receipt of a finished specification
    → Declare Layer 4 design obligations before authoring any manifest: identify the compliance_scope,
      path_id, environment, and team label values for all NetworkPolicy and ServiceAccount resources,
      and confirm the {path_id}-{service_name}-sa ServiceAccount naming convention
    → Confirm cluster prerequisites:
        cert-manager + ClusterIssuer 'gainwell-enterprise-issuer' deployed
        Azure Workload Identity enabled
        GP-001 workload_identity_ref (managed identity client ID for AKS / IAM role ARN for EKS) confirmed from PTN-INFRA-GOV-003 Phase 6 output
        Kafka broker CIDRs and Key Vault endpoint CIDRs confirmed with networking team

Phase 2: Security Template Root
    → Create catalog/security-templates/{path-id}/security-template-manifest.yaml
        Declare compliance scope, required manifest list, OPA check ID references
    → Create catalog/security-templates/{path-id}/manifests/

Phase 3: Network Policy (OPA-001, OPA-002)
    → Author networkpolicy.yaml with deny-all default + explicit ingress/egress allowlist
    → Run: opa eval --data policy-bundle/ --input networkpolicy.yaml 'data.gp001.opa001.allow'
    → Run: opa eval --data policy-bundle/ --input networkpolicy.yaml 'data.gp001.opa002.allow'
    → Both must return true before proceeding

Phase 4: TLS Certificate (OPA-004)
    → Author certificate.yaml with ClusterIssuer reference and correct dnsNames
    → Run: opa eval --data policy-bundle/ --input certificate.yaml 'data.gp001.opa004.allow'
    → Must return true before proceeding

Phase 5: ServiceAccount + Workload Identity (OPA-005)
    → Author serviceaccount.yaml with azure.workload.identity/client-id annotation
    → Run: opa eval --data policy-bundle/ --input serviceaccount.yaml 'data.gp001.opa005.allow'
    → Coordinate with scaffold author: confirm deployment.yaml securityContext has all 6 fields
    → Run: opa eval --data policy-bundle/ --input deployment.yaml 'data.gp001.opa003.allow'
    → Run: opa eval --data policy-bundle/ --input deployment.yaml 'data.gp001.opa006.allow'
    → All three must return true before proceeding

Phase 6: Pod Security Admission (OPA-007)
    → Author podsecurity-patch.yaml namespace patch
    → Confirm PSA 'restricted' label syntax against cluster Kubernetes version
    → Apply to staging namespace; confirm enforcement active via: kubectl get ns {namespace} --show-labels
    → Run: opa eval --data policy-bundle/ --input namespace.yaml 'data.gp001.opa007.allow'

Phase 7: Security Architecture Review
    → Schedule Security Architecture session with: OPA check YAML, all manifests, compliance scope declaration
    → Walk through each OPA check and the manifest field satisfying it
    → Obtain written sign-off

Phase 8: Layer 2 Fitness Functions, Validation, Evidence, and ARB Submission
    → Deploy merged manifest set to staging environment; confirm all resources reach a ready state
    → Run Layer 2a Network Isolation fitness function:
        Send test request from unauthorized namespace to staged workload
        Confirm NetworkPolicy blocks the request (expected: ECONNREFUSED or 403 from network layer)
        Save result as: network-isolation-{path-id}-{version}.txt
    → Run Layer 2b Certificate Issuance fitness function:
        kubectl get certificate -n {namespace} {service-name}-tls -o yaml
        Confirm status.conditions: type=Ready, status="True"
        Confirm spec.issuerRef.name matches gainwell-enterprise-issuer (not selfsigned-issuer)
        Save output as: cert-issuance-{path-id}-{version}.txt
    → Submit network-isolation-*.txt and cert-issuance-*.txt to compliance evidence store
        Minimum retention: 3 years for HIPAA and FedRAMP Moderate paths
    → Run full OPA eval against merged manifest set (scaffold + security template):
        opa eval --data policy-bundle/ --input manifests/ 'data.gp001'
    → All OPA-001 through OPA-007 must return allow: true
    → Save OPA evaluation output as opa-evidence-{path-id}-{version}.json
    → Submit opa-evidence-*.json to compliance evidence store
    → Run conformance-check --validate-scaffold: Layer 1 file presence checks must pass
    → Confirm staging deployment: ESO syncs secrets, pod runs as non-root (kubectl exec -- id)
    → ARB submission package must include:
        security-template-manifest.yaml
        network-isolation-{path-id}-{version}.txt (Layer 2a result)
        cert-issuance-{path-id}-{version}.txt (Layer 2b result)
        opa-evidence-{path-id}-{version}.json (Layer 3 result)
        policy toolchain version
```

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#opa-check-reference-table]

### OPA Check Reference Table

For each OPA check that the security template must satisfy, the following table maps the check to the specific manifest field and the validation command:

| Check ID | Assertion | Manifest | Field | OPA Rule Path |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| OPA-001 | `NetworkPolicy` with service `podSelector` exists | `networkpolicy.yaml` | `spec.podSelector.matchLabels.app` | `data.gp001.opa001.allow` |
| OPA-002 | Egress CIDRs restricted to approved list | `networkpolicy.yaml` | `spec.egress[].to[].ipBlock.cidr` | `data.gp001.opa002.allow` |
| OPA-003 | `runAsNonRoot: true` in all containers | `deployment.yaml` | `spec.template.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot` | `data.gp001.opa003.allow` |
| OPA-004 | Certificate issuer is `gainwell-enterprise-issuer` | `certificate.yaml` | `spec.issuerRef.name` | `data.gp001.opa004.allow` |
| OPA-005 | ServiceAccount non-default, workload identity annotated | `serviceaccount.yaml` | `metadata.name`, `metadata.annotations[azure.workload.identity/client-id]` | `data.gp001.opa005.allow` |
| OPA-006 | `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` in all containers | `deployment.yaml` | `spec.template.spec.containers[].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation` | `data.gp001.opa006.allow` |
| OPA-007 | Namespace PSA label = `restricted` | namespace object | `metadata.labels[pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce]` | `data.gp001.opa007.allow` |

### Pre-Submission Checklist

| Layer 1 file presence checks pass in `conformance-check --validate-scaffold` | Layer 1 — Structural Conformance | ☐ |
| Layer 2a Network Isolation fitness function passed; result saved as `network-isolation-{path-id}-{version}.txt` | Layer 2 — Fitness Function | ☐ |
| Layer 2b Certificate Issuance fitness function passed (`Ready=True`, correct issuer); result saved as `cert-issuance-{path-id}-{version}.txt` | Layer 2 — Fitness Function | ☐ |
| `network-isolation-*.txt` and `cert-issuance-*.txt` submitted to compliance evidence store | Layer 2 — Evidence Store | ☐ |
| All OPA-001 through OPA-007 return `allow: true` in `opa eval` run | Layer 3 — Policy-as-Code | ☐ |
| OPA eval output saved as `opa-evidence-{path-id}-{version}.json` and submitted to compliance evidence store | Layer 3 — Evidence Store | ☐ |
| OPA assertions co-defined with Verification Contract author (not received as a finished spec) | Layer 3 — Co-authoring | ☐ |
| `compliance_scope`, `path_id`, `environment`, `team` labels declared on NetworkPolicy and ServiceAccount | Layer 4 — Runtime Monitor Design | ☐ |
| ServiceAccount named `{path_id}-{service_name}-sa` | Layer 4 — Runtime Monitor Design | ☐ |
| `networkpolicy.yaml` has deny-all default and explicit ingress + egress allowlist | — | ☐ |
| `certificate.yaml` references `gainwell-enterprise-issuer` ClusterIssuer by exact name | — | ☐ |
| `serviceaccount.yaml` has `azure.workload.identity/client-id` annotation with non-empty value | — | ☐ |
| `deployment.yaml` has all six securityContext fields (confirmed with scaffold author) | — | ☐ |
| `podsecurity-patch.yaml` applies `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` | — | ☐ |

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#decision-point-1-network-policy--allowlist-or-denylist-approach]

#### Decision Point 1: Network Policy — Allowlist or Denylist Approach?

**Context:** Should the NetworkPolicy use an explicit allowlist (deny all, permit specific) or a denylist (permit all, deny specific)?

**Options:**
- Allowlist: `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` with no default rule means deny-all; explicit `ingress:` and `egress:` stanzas are the allowlist
- Denylist: Not applicable — Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is inherently allowlist-only; policy rules add permissions, they do not remove them from an existing permit-all baseline

**Recommendation:** Always use the allowlist approach (deny-all by default via `policyTypes` without a default allow stanza). Kubernetes NetworkPolicy semantics guarantee deny-all when `policyTypes` is declared with no matching stanza. This is the only correct approach for HIPAA network isolation.
page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#decision-point-2-certificate-duration--how-long]

#### Decision Point 2: Certificate Duration — How Long?

**Context:** cert-manager `Certificate` duration and `renewBefore` defaults. Longer duration reduces renewal operations; shorter duration reduces the window of a compromised certificate.

**Options:**
- 90-day duration (Let's Encrypt default): Higher operational overhead from frequent renewals; aligns with modern certificate lifespan recommendations
- 1-year duration (GP-001 default): Lower operational overhead; still within acceptable bounds for enterprise internal certificates issued by the enterprise CA

**Recommendation:** Use 1-year duration with 30-day `renewBefore` for internal services using the `gainwell-enterprise-issuer` ClusterIssuer. For services exposed to external traffic, align with the CISO's certificate policy. The `renewBefore` period of 30 days provides adequate time for manual intervention if cert-manager renewal fails before the certificate expires.
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#decision-point-3-what-if-the-application-scaffolds-deploymentyaml-is-missing-securitycontext]

#### Decision Point 3: What if the Application Scaffold's `deployment.yaml` is Missing `securityContext`?

**Context:** The scaffold author is responsible for `deployment.yaml` but the security template author needs to validate that securityContext fields are present for OPA-003 and OPA-006 to pass.

**Options:**
- Add securityContext to the security template manifests as a `deployment.yaml` patch
- Block security template submission until the scaffold is updated
- Accept the gap and note it in the ARB submission as a known deficiency

**Recommendation:** Block — do not submit a security template to the ARB if the corresponding scaffold's `deployment.yaml` is missing required securityContext fields. The security template and scaffold are reviewed as a bundle. A security template that passes OPA-001 through OPA-007 in isolation but fails when validated against the actual scaffold output does not provide the security assurance it claims. Coordinate the scaffold update first; submit together.

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#example-1-authoring-the-gp-001-security-template]

### Example 1: Authoring the GP-001 Security Template

**Context:** Platform Engineering is authoring the GP-001 security template. The Verification Contract defines OPA-001 through OPA-007. The cluster has cert-manager with `gainwell-enterprise-issuer`, Azure Workload Identity enabled, and the Kafka CIDR confirmed as `10.0.8.0/24`.

**Phase 3 (Network Policy):** Author `networkpolicy.yaml` with deny-all, ingress from `ingress-nginx` namespace on port 8080, egress to Kubernetes DNS on UDP 53, Key Vault on TCP 443, and Kafka on TCP 9093. Run `opa eval` — OPA-001 passes (NetworkPolicy with `app: $service_name` selector), OPA-002 passes (egress CIDRs match approved list).

**Phase 4 (Certificate):** Author `certificate.yaml` with `issuerRef.name: gainwell-enterprise-issuer`. Run `opa eval` — OPA-004 passes (issuer is `gainwell-enterprise-issuer`, not `selfsigned`).

**Phase 5 (ServiceAccount):** Author `serviceaccount.yaml` with client-id annotation. Coordinate with scaffold author: confirm `deployment.yaml` has all six securityContext fields. Run `opa eval` — OPA-003, OPA-005, OPA-006 all pass.

**Phase 6 (PSA):** Apply PSA patch to staging namespace. Confirm label present. OPA-007 passes.

**Phase 7 (Security Architecture review):** Security Architecture reviews CIDR ranges, issuer reference, workload identity client ID. Sign-off obtained.

**Phase 8 (Layer 2 Fitness Functions, Validation, and ARB Submission):** Merged artifact set applied to staging. Layer 2a network isolation fitness function run — test request from unauthorized namespace is blocked; result saved as `network-isolation-GP-001-v1.0.0.txt` and submitted to evidence store. Layer 2b certificate issuance fitness function run — `kubectl get certificate` confirms `Ready=True` with `issuerRef.name: gainwell-enterprise-issuer`; result saved as `cert-issuance-GP-001-v1.0.0.txt` and submitted to evidence store. Full `opa eval` run — all seven checks pass; output saved as `opa-evidence-GP-001-v1.0.0.json` and submitted to evidence store. Staging deployment confirms ESO sync and pod runs as UID 1000. ARB package includes the three evidence files, `security-template-manifest.yaml`, and policy toolchain version.

**Outcome:** 12 minutes from OPA validation to Security Architecture sign-off. ARB approves the complete bundle. The first 6 services instantiated from GP-001 enter production with all OPA checks pre-satisfied.

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#example-2-adding-fedramp-controls-to-an-existing-path]

### Example 2: Adding FedRAMP Controls to an Existing Path

**Context:** GP-001 (HIPAA) is being extended to GP-007 (FedRAMP Moderate). The FedRAMP addition requires FIPS 140-2 compliant cipher suites and stricter egress controls.

**Change to security template:**
- `certificate.yaml`: Add TLS cipher suite annotation to the Certificate resource restricting to FIPS-approved algorithms
- `networkpolicy.yaml`: Remove the Kafka egress rule (FedRAMP scope does not use the shared audit event bus; a dedicated FedRAMP audit bus is used)
- New OPA check: `OPA-008` — TLS cipher suites restricted to FIPS-approved list
- `security-template-manifest.yaml`: Update compliance scope to `['HIPAA', 'FedRAMP-Moderate']`

**Process:** Security Architecture review covers both the HIPAA base controls and the FedRAMP additions. ARB approves GP-007 as a new path (not a version bump of GP-001 — different compliance scope).

[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-001-golden-path-security-template-authoring-guidance.md#approval-process]

### Approval Process

The security template is not submitted to the ARB independently. It is part of the complete Golden Path bundle. Security Architecture review is a prerequisite for ARB submission — the ARB does not perform the technical security review. Security template updates that add or change OPA checks require both Security Architecture review and ARB notification regardless of version type. There is no lightweight minor-version path for security control changes.
